justification_text:
The point estimates at each time horizon (1-day, 1-week, and 1-month) were primarily driven by the underlying trend in the data up to the time of the forecast, as well as recent patterns in volatility and any short-term factors that were influencing the system. For the 1-day forecast, I leaned more heavily on recent behavior since day-to-day changes tend to be more manageable to project with relatively higher certainty based on immediate trends. For the 1-week forecast, the point estimate began to incorporate the mean-reverting tendencies or expected corrective movements that might emerge over a slightly longer term. For 1-month, the point estimate reflected a broader trend, factoring in projections of where the system is heading if trends and external factors continue without major disruption.

The width of the confidence intervals grows as the forecast horizon increases because uncertainty accumulates over time. For the 1-day projection, uncertainty is lower because fewer variables can influence outcomes in that short window. By 1 week, uncertainty increases as underlying drivers, like market shifts or random noise, have more time to play out. At the 1-month horizon, uncertainty widens significantly because more unknowns—structural changes in the system, external shocks, or compounding effects—can arise. This escalation in uncertainty is why the 90% confidence interval grows substantially from the 1-day to the 1-month forecast.

Specific risks or events could push outcomes outside of the stated confidence intervals, especially at longer horizons. Sudden, unexpected events—like geopolitical developments, major policy changes, economic shocks, or unexpected data releases—could shift the trajectory in ways that are not currently embedded within the forecast. For example, a severe market correction or a major announcement could push values far beyond the upper or lower bounds of the 1-week or 1-month intervals. At the 1-day horizon, outcomes are less sensitive to large disruptions but could still be influenced by things like unusually high trading activity or unexpected announcements. While the confidence intervals are designed to account for most expected variation, these types of tail-risk events could lead to outcomes outside the forecasted ranges.
